nigeria_now: Active insurgency (Boko Haram/ISWAP), banditry, farmer-herder violence; ACLED political-violence fatalities ~9,896 (2024) and ~12,881 (2025), a decade high; state cannot project authority across NW/NE
analogues_at_stage: US had frontier violence + a civil war (1861-65); Korea had the Korean War (1950-53) THEN decades of order; China had Mao-era upheaval THEN post-1978 stability. Their catch-up GROWTH ran AFTER violence resolved into a monopoly on force
note: Not that analogues were peaceful - they were violent - but their high growth phase FOLLOWED the restoration of order. Nigeria's insecurity is CONCURRENT with its would-be takeoff and is territorial (lost writ over regions), which taxes investment, farming and human capital exactly where growth must come from

nigeria_now: WGI Rule of Law -1.01 (2024), ~12th-15th percentile; control of corruption and government effectiveness similarly ~-1; rent-extracting corruption sits atop LOW state capacity
analogues_at_stage: Korea under Park (1960s-70s) was authoritarian and corrupt BUT had a Weberian bureaucracy (Economic Planning Board) and 'embedded/growth-enhancing' corruption disciplined by export targets; US Gilded Age was graft-ridden but had courts, secure property rights and rule of law
note: The decisive contrast is not corruption's PRESENCE (all had it) but its TYPE plus state capacity. Korea's rents were performance-conditioned and reinvested; Nigeria's are extractive and capital-flight-prone atop a weak bureaucracy that cannot enforce contracts or collect tax (non-oil revenue/GDP among world's lowest)

nigeria_now: Oil = ~88% of exports and roughly half of federation revenue; textbook Dutch disease - real exchange-rate/rent bias crowds out tradable agriculture and manufacturing; rentier fiscal base
analogues_at_stage: The Asian tigers (Korea, Taiwan) were resource-POOR - a hidden blessing that FORCED them to export manufactures to earn FX. US/UK/Germany had coal/iron but as INPUTS to an industrial base, not a rentier substitute for one
note: Resource poverty was a catalyst for the tigers; resource wealth is a trap for Nigeria. Oil gives the state income without needing a productive citizenry or broad tax bargain, weakening both accountability and the non-oil tradable sector that drives catch-up

nigeria_now: TFR ~4.4-5.0; median age ~17-18; ~2.4%/yr population growth; dividend NOT yet captured because fertility has fallen only slowly, keeping the dependency ratio high
analogues_at_stage: Korea's TFR fell 6.1 (1960) to ~2.0 (1982) - a sharp transition that produced a large working-age bulge with few dependents; ~1/3 of the East Asian miracle growth is attributed to this fast fertility drop. China's one-child era did the same
note: Double-edged: the youth bulge is LATENT dividend fuel and gives Nigeria a huge domestic market the small tigers lacked. But without a fast fertility decline AND jobs, fast population growth DILUTES per-capita gains and turns the bulge into unemployment/instability. Dividend is delayed and shallow, currently being squandered - the one factor that could flip favourable if fertility falls and jobs appear

nigeria_now: ~18.3m out-of-school children (10.2m primary, 8.1m secondary); ~74% of 7-14s lack basic reading/math; life expectancy ~62
analogues_at_stage: Korea at 1960 takeoff had ~72% adult literacy and near-universal primary enrolment by the late 1960s (post-war land reform + 'education fever'); China had near-universal primary and ~66% literacy by the early 1980s reform onset
note: Korea/China entered their high-growth decades with a broadly literate, healthy workforce READY to absorb factory work and rising skill. Nigeria's foundational-skills deficit and out-of-school stock mean the labour force is not yet equipped to climb a productivity ladder even if one existed

nigeria_now: Manufacturing ~8-9% of GDP (fell from ~9.3% in 2023); services ~46-58%; urbanizing and shifting to services WITHOUT a manufacturing phase
analogues_at_stage: Korea and China INDUSTRIALIZED first - manufacturing reached ~25-35% of GDP at peak, absorbing rural labour into rising-productivity factory jobs before pivoting to services
note: Rodrik's premature deindustrialization: the manufacturing 'escalator' now peaks earlier and at far lower income than for early industrializers. Nigeria is losing the one sector that historically delivered scalable, tradable, productivity-raising jobs; urbanization-without-industrialization yields informal low-productivity services, not catch-up

nigeria_now: Faces deglobalization (world trade/GDP plateaued/falling since ~2008), automation/robots eroding the low-wage manufacturing ladder, and severe climate exposure (ND-GAIN ~161/182; shrinking Lake Chad; Sahel desertification)
analogues_at_stage: Korea/China caught up DURING hyper-globalization: world trade/GDP surged ~37% (1986) to ~61% (2008); China's 2001 WTO accession opened vast export markets and offshoring flows just as it industrialized
note: Tailwind then vs headwind now. The export-manufacturing route that lifted the tigers is being automated and reshored away before Nigeria can board it, and climate stress hits its agriculture and North directly. Partial offsets: digital-services export, fintech/leapfrogging and 'japa' remittances - but these do not replace the mass-employment ladder that is closing
